/case-studies/hope-house.title: Anonymity by Design | Hope House NGO App
/case-studies/hope-house.description: Designing a mental health support app for an NGO where the central decision was making anonymity the default, not an afterthought.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
A safe place to ask what you can't ask
An NGO in Vellore came to us with something genuinely hard: adolescents had no secure, credible place to get information about the world they were growing up in, or about themselves.

The problem wasn't scarcity; it was the opposite. Information overload, uneven credibility, and a social context where asking certain questions out loud carries real cost. In an orthodox society a teenager can't ask a parent about half of what they need to know. So they don't ask, or they ask the internet and take whatever it gives them.
On a team of five; everyone else was a developer. Identity, user flows, design system, all screens.
The design system stayed deliberately plain; clean readable type, soothing simple palette, scalable to both mobile and web. It's a text-heavy product about difficult things. Restraint was the point.

We wanted warm, welcoming, and instantly recognisable. We played with a simple "H" for recognition and a house for safety, and the final mark combines them — the letter sitting inside the shape. The idea underneath: your house is your hope.
The whole product turns on one choice: anonymity is the feature, not a setting.

Every instinct in social product design pushes toward identity: profiles, reputation, follower counts, the things that drive engagement. All of them would have destroyed this. A teenager asking something they're afraid to ask their parents will not attach their name to it, however good the answer is.
So the entire experience sits behind an anonymous cloak by default. No profile-building, no social capital, no reason to perform

Reading a post and asking a question are different emotional acts; one is passive and safe, the other takes nerve. Collapsing them into one feed would have made asking feel more exposed than it needed to. The design system draws a clear line, and the product has exactly two tabs.

A post a day, by category. Pets, relationships, sexuality, language, whatever the NGO identified as needed. Every post carries its source, so users know where information came from. A short AI summary for the gist, full article for depth. A calendar so you can reach any day's post, at your own pace.
The design system stayed deliberately plain — clean readable type, soothing simple palette, scalable to both mobile and web. It's a text-heavy product about difficult things. Restraint was the point.

Browse what others have asked, filtered by category, answered by verified NGO professionals. Ask your own in one tap. The system auto-categorises so it routes to the right person, with manual override if it guesses wrong.

Almost every engagement pattern I knew would have made this product worse. Sometimes the job is knowing which best practices to throw out; and I'd like to say I knew that going in, but honestly the NGO knew their users better than I did and I mostly had the sense to listen.

/case-studies/poll-police.title: Designing for 70M+ Voters | Poll Police, Tamil Nadu
/case-studies/poll-police.description: A Flutter app built with the Tamil Nadu Police and Government of India, serving three voter, officer, and administrator roles across 70M+ people.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
Google Developer Group VIT × Government of India
Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip or 30 second video to understand this project?
The Tamil Nadu Police came to us; me and four others from the Google Developer Group at VIT, where I was Community Lead. With a problem they'd identified themselves.

Two things were going wrong: People didn't reliably know where to go to vote. And in a lot of places, people didn't feel safe going; violence and pressure around polling stations were real, and the information gap made it worse. Police had their own problem: officers working the same election couldn't easily see what other officers were seeing.
We went into the field and talked to officers and to people across Tamil Nadu — specifically about what devices they were actually holding, because that would define everything else.

Two findings shaped the whole build. Tamil Nadu is linguistically diverse, so text-heavy interfaces exclude people by default; visuals are understood universally. And the device reality across 70 million+ people skewed heavily toward older, low-powered phones.
Find your polling station, know when it's safe. Select a district from a list or a map, zoom in, tap a station, get everything.
Navigate the city, track police vehicles, coordinate coverage.
Oversee the operation, manage resources, see the whole picture.
We built in Flutter and designed against the worst device in the field, not the best.
Designed for the worst devices on market

That killed a lot of otherwise-good ideas early: heavy maps, rich media, anything assuming a modern handset or a stable connection. Flutter let us serve both older low-power devices and the web from one codebase, which mattered more than any individual feature would have.
Each of the three districts got its own theme, held consistently across backgrounds and containers, with contrast tuned so even plain black text stayed effortlessly readable.
That sounds cosmetic. It isn't. An officer glancing at a colleague's screen knows the district instantly, without asking. Mid-election, that removes an entire category of miscommunication.

Three districts shipped. We designed for seventy million and deployed to a fraction of that, and I've never fully stopped thinking about the gap. Also I'd fight harder for a proper offline mode. We optimised for weak connections but never truly designed for no connection, which on election day in rural Tamil Nadu is not an edge case.

/case-studies/divergent-minds-convergent.title: Divergent Minds, Convergent Design | UX Research
/case-studies/divergent-minds-convergent.description: A research study on how designers from artistic versus non-artistic backgrounds spot usability issues, based on 8 interviews across 4 backgrounds.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?

Every UX practitioner has heard the Henry Ford line: "if I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses." It gets used to justify not listening to users. I wanted to find out whether it actually holds up.

So I ran a study. Eight people across four backgrounds: designers, developers and PMs, artistic non-designers, non-artistic non-designers; all looking at the same two interface screens, while I measured how fast they found problems, how many they found, and what they chose to care about.

The findings surprised me in places. Artistic background mattered more than industry experience. General users weren't blind to design — they simply cared about what a product gave them rather than how it looked. And the industry appears to make designers more critical and, uncomfortably, more conformist.

/case-studies/airtel.title: Redesigning a Merchant App for 1M+ Users | Airtel
/case-studies/airtel.description: Simplifying a cluttered merchant app for non-tech-savvy users on low-power devices, cutting feature-discovery time by 14%.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
Desiging for tech with lower power
The merchant app had 60+ features that people used regularly. All of them were on the home screen, because nobody had decided what mattered more than anything else.

Worse: it had been designed for desktop. The actual users were shopkeepers on low-powered Android phones with small screens, many with limited formal education, using this between serving customers not sitting at a desk. Dense desktop UI, tiny screens, text-heavy navigation, low reading comfort. Every constraint pointing the same way.
Colleagues had already collected field data on how merchants used the platform. I dug into it for what was used most, what was dead weight, and whether anyone customised anything. Mostly they didn't.
Do they search? Browse categories? Set favourites? Range widely or return to the same few things?
The finding that shaped everything: most merchants use two or three features constantly and almost nothing else.

The tempting move was to surface the top features and bury the rest. I didn't ; "the rest" still mattered to someone, and a feature used by 5% of a million merchants is fifty thousand people. I also stuck tightly to company design standards rather than inventing a new visual language. In an app handling people's money, familiarity is trust.

Favourites and recently-used pinned to the top, then categories acting as filters over a running list, not folders you enter and exit. A merchant who only ever uses two things never navigates at all. Someone hunting across categories moves across categories rather than scanning all options

A distinct style was created for an audience that is not very education plus every merchant talks in a different language. Icons were considered universally easy to understand and 100+ custom icons were created to represent sections of the application.
With a measurable drop in support load.

Looking back at these icons I'm worried about scalability. Would they translate to phone screens with super small zoomed-out content? I designed them at a comfortable size on a comfortable screen; which is exactly the mistake the original desktop-first app made. I should have considered talking to the design system team to understand the reasons behind such choices.

/case-studies/group-alarm.title: Group Alarm | Solo-Built App, 1,000+ Downloads
/case-studies/group-alarm.description: A solo-designed and built alarm app in Framer that lets one toggle disable an entire group of alarms at once. 1,000+ downloads, 20+ reviews.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
A celebrity posted a screenshot of their alarms. A gazillion of them, no structure, one for every conceivable purpose.
And I thought: why do we organise our files, our photos, our email and not this? Why not sets of alarms for different kinds of days?
I have five alarms between 6:45 and 7:30 so that I'm actually up by 7:30. You probably have something similar. Every alarm app treats those five as five unrelated objects.
One on, One off. Wake me at 6 tomorrow, I have a thing.
Schedule-driven, repeating, and almost never actually one alarm. Get me up for work. In practice: 6:45, 6:55, 7:05, 7:15, 7:30. Five alarms, one intention.
Ideas (everything, good or bad), Product Goals (merged into real-world actions), Users (scenarios)
The design question was where to put the weight. Groups are the real behaviour, but single alarms are the more frequent action; you add a one-off far more often than you build a new group.
The app works exactly like the one you already know, and added groups as the thing on top for people who want the structure. Familiar first, innovation optional.
Adding a normal alarm stays as fast as it's ever been. Groups are a deliberate construct: name one ("Morning run"), see every alarm inside it, edit one or change something across all of them.
And the piece that made it worth building: toggle an entire group off in one action. Not running this week? One switch. Five separate alarms could never give you that.

Type and colour tuned for legibility, because people scan long alarm lists rather than reading them. And each group gets its own theme; so you know which group you're in without reading its name. Visual cues doing the work that labels would otherwise have to.
Setting alarms isn't a daily activity, so every screen had to be efficient rather than beautiful. Mostly.

Sponsorship converting in-app coins into real investable money · partnerships with investment platforms or advisors to bridge learning and doing · a full curriculum for schools · micro-credentials people can share professionally.

The best thing that happened here was a concept failing in front of ten people, early, before we'd fallen in love with it. I'd want that failure even earlier now; we built wireframes before we tested the format, and paper would have told us the same thing a week sooner.

/case-studies/moneylingo.title: MoneyLingo | Design Thinking Case Study, UT Austin
/case-studies/moneylingo.description: A financial literacy app that pivoted from a board game to a quiz and stock simulation after testing showed the game felt too stressful.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
Millennials carry disproportionate debt and low savings compared to older generations. So: teach people to build wealth.

We spoke to students and young adults about loans, investments, debt, and how they learned any of it. They worried most about being beholden to repayment, or being taken advantage of. Their approaches to investing varied wildly.
They got financial information, answers ranged from "friends and family" to "the internet" — specifically reddit.
Ideas (everything, good or bad), Product Goals (merged into real-world actions), Users (scenarios)
It was that personal finance knowledge isn't accessible from anywhere reliable, especially for students and people feel judged asking, so they don't.
A graduate student who wants to secure himself financially, needs a way to approach financial decision-making, because everyone around him says something different.

We explored a range, from a board game to an educational app offering a safe space to talk about money. We built deliberately plain low-fidelity wireframes — keeping execution ugly so feedback landed on the idea.

Users liked the idea of a game but found the board game confusing and enormous in scope. The app tested better on two specific grounds: it was easy to learn and it reached more people easily. We kept the mechanic and threw away the format.
The design decision I'd defend hardest: the feedback loop never punishes you.

The learning flow is three actions — Learning → Answering → Feedback. Learning and answering are a quiz. But feedback is built to show what you need to work on while cheering you on for what you got right. Never a negative framing.

That's not softness. Our entire research finding was that people avoid this topic because they feel judged. A product that marked them down at every question would have rebuilt the exact problem it existed to solve.
Blue and dark blue, calm and professional; chosen specifically so people wouldn't drop off over the trust anxiety that money products carry. Type: Lato, across the whole platform.

Onboarding kept simple and playful, with questions to tailor the experience without overloading anyone up front. A homepage tying the parts together. A statistics-based profile so progress is comparable.
Post-feedback changes: navigation visuals, a better introduction to the stock practice flow, more context on onboarding questions, and section-level explanations to kill confusion.

Sponsorship converting in-app coins into real investable money · partnerships with investment platforms or advisors to bridge learning and doing · a full curriculum for schools · micro-credentials people can share professionally.

The best thing that happened here was a concept failing in front of ten people, early, before we'd fallen in love with it. I'd want that failure even earlier now; we built wireframes before we tested the format, and paper would have told us the same thing a week sooner.

/case-studies/paytm-chat.title: Designing Trust Into Payments | Paytm Chat Case Study
/case-studies/paytm-chat.description: Designing chat-payments primitives from zero for 500M+ users, where every component needed legal and compliance sign-off before it could ship.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?

I joined Paytm in 2020, right as UPI; India's real-time payments rail was reshaping the market. Paytm had been the default way to send money in India for years. Then Google Pay integrated UPI and added something Paytm didn't have: you could chat with someone while paying them. Users started migrating.
Paytm's answer was to bring that same idea to its own homepage: a surface that over 500 million people touch every month. Whatever shipped there wasn't a feature update. It was a brand statement.

We didn't just want chat-plus-payments. We wanted to go further than Google Pay had: bill splitting, group chats, group savings pools, and eventually using the same surface for conversations about investing — UPI as a starting point, not the whole idea.
Every component we built had to go back into Paytm's core design system; which meant every one of them needed legal, business, and management sign-off before it shipped.

Paytm had never had chat before. There was no bubble style, no message-state pattern, nothing to extend: we were defining primitives for the first time, in a domain (payments) that's about as regulated as consumer software gets in India. That's a real constraint most chat products never face: a "send" button isn't just a UX decision, it's a compliance conversation.

So we built deliberately, in public, with each new piece: chat bubbles, image sends, video sends, money sends, combinations of all of them checked at every stage rather than designed in a vacuum and approved at the end. Message states got the same treatment: sent, delivered, read, and reacted-to, each with distinct, tested visual treatment.

A full chat-and-payments experience on Paytm's homepage: text, image, video, and money in one conversation thread, group chat with bill-splitting and group savings, and a foundation meant to eventually carry investment conversations too. A new component category added permanently to Paytm's design system, not a one-off feature.
The obvious solution is a form: enter amounts, assign people, send requests. We wanted something that felt like what splitting a bill actually feels like.

So we built a pizza visualization: a shared bill shown as a pizza divided into slices (eight, in our design), portioned across three or four people based on who owed what share. Adjust the slices, adjust the payment split. It turned a financial form into something that looked like what you were actually doing at the table.

Paytm Chat launched with a set of custom illustrated stickers. Built with the motion team, so sending money could carry an emotion, not just a transaction. Send someone money, and the interface could react automatically.
Every send also triggered an instant confirmation message stating exactly how much was sent and how fast. A small, deliberate detail proving Paytm's core promise: this is instant.
Ideas (everything, good or bad), Product Goals (merged into real-world actions), Users (scenarios)

Post-launch, the team ran A/B tests through CleverTap with the research team to refine the experience further — I'd moved to Paytm's design systems team by that point, so I can speak to what shipped, not to how those later tests changed it.

We designed every message state (sent, delivered, read, reacted) in real depth, and I still think that level of care is why the experience felt trustworthy fast in a category (payments) where trust is the entire game.

If I did it again, I'd push to stay through the A/B testing phase. I built the foundation and handed off before seeing what the data actually said about it, and that's the one part of this project I never got to close the loop on.

/case-studies/winuall.title: Designing for Two Audiences at Once | Winuall Case Study
/case-studies/winuall.description: A freelance ed-tech app with light mode default for students and dark mode default for teachers, designed around when each actually uses it.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip or 30 second video to understand this project?

COVID broke Indian education overnight. A huge amount of teaching; especially outside major cities ran on paper. Notebooks, printed papers, physical submissions. When classrooms closed, that had nowhere to go.

Winuall was the bridge: get paper-based coaching institutes online without assuming anyone involved was comfortable with digital anything. We worked with institutes each serving thousands of students, all of them rooted in decades of traditional methods.
Design system, landing page, web portal, student mobile app, admin mobile app, illustrations, icons, tutorials.

The interesting problem: the same system had to serve teenagers and their teachers, and those two groups want opposite things. Students disengage from anything institutional. Teachers distrust anything that feels like a toy. Most people would split it ; two systems, two languages. I kept one and made it flex: type leaning playful, colour staying clean and formal. Vibrancy where engagement mattered, restraint where credibility did.

Light mode by default for students, dark mode by default for teachers. Not aesthetic; scheduling. Students use this during the day, in class, and a dark interface in daylight pushed them toward drowsy. Teachers use it at night, after they've finished teaching, when a bright screen is punishing. Both could switch. Most didn't need to.

Tutorials as a layer inside the product, not a one-time onboarding tour. These users were moving from notebooks to software with no prior mental model. A skippable intro would have been useless. Guidance had to live where people actually got stuc; and we iterated on it with institute administrators until it clicked.
Every institute had its own way of doing things and change wasn't their strong suit. Most of the portal could be reshaped to match.
Colour-coded actions in the admin app, so similar tasks couldn't be confused mid-tap.
We found this audience loved double-checking their work. Popups and notifications throughout, confirming what had just happened.

The product suite supported by the adapative design system was shipped out for 3 major education institutes helping cover 12,000 local students and having a reach of 500,000+ user base projected in the next ten years,

I built four products and one design system as one person, and the system carried it. But I'd document the customisation rules far more tightly now; I made it flexible without defining where flexibility stops, which is how design systems quietly become suggestions.

/case-studies/snapshot.title: Snapshot | Interaction Design Case Study, UT Austin
/case-studies/snapshot.description: A content-first photo app that deliberately excluded a social feed, raising SUS scores from 76.25 to 82.27 through iterative testing.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
Real-time feedback while you shoot, not after

There are hundreds of photo apps, and almost none of them help you take a better photo. Every suggestion arrives afterwards, in edit mode; which is exactly the wrong moment. The critical time is while you're holding the camera up.

Our starting concept came from a shared interest in music, photography, and film: recreate famous photos and movie scenes based on where you're standing. That grew into something wider: templates, pose guidance, and real-time feedback.

With people across a range of photography skill, friends and family included. What devices, when they shoot, what frustrates them.People overwhelmingly use phones, shoot most when travelling or somewhere new, and want something nice enough to share — but not everyone's a professional and the effort is real.
80+ responses, asking what apps they use, what their goals are, which features they'd want, and to rank those features. We selected nine essential features from it.
Ideas (everything, good or bad), Product Goals (merged into real-world actions), Users (scenarios)
Across Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, VSCO, AiryCam, and Ulike confirmed the gap: nobody was doing real-time guidance during capture.

For a photo app this is close to heresy; social is the obvious growth engine, and every competitor we studied leaned on it. We chose content creation over social networking and deliberately left the feed out. The product does one thing: help you take a better picture. Adding a feed would have made it a worse version of six apps that already exist.
WE KEPT TEMPLATES CONTRARY TO SURVEY RESULTS

Only 38% ranked photo/video templates as high priority, under our own bar. We kept the feature anyway, because it was the differentiator and because a survey measures what people can imagine, not what they'd use once it existed. The concept tests backed that up: pose recommendations and spot suggestions were what people responded to most.
Eight sketches each in eight minutes, then presenting to find common themes. Camera flow, search, and map integration surfaced immediately.
Then wireframes, then concept testing with hand-drawn sketches deliberately kept rough so people understood it was a work in progress and felt free to criticise it.

Moderated usability testing over Zoom and Figma, thinking aloud. SUS: 76.25. Above the 68 average, not good enough. We fixed four things: specific search instructions like "Search Barton Springs", a progress indicator, clearer real-time feedback, and a browsing function in maps.

Building upon our mid-fidelity screens, we elevated the design to a high-fidelity level. We developed a design system, incorporating a color palette and iconography for a cohesive visual identity. High-fidelity screens aimed to enhance the app's visual appeal while maintaining user-friendliness.

With high-fidelity screens in place, we conducted unmoderated usability testing using UserTesting.com. This phase involved 10 participants who completed specific tasks within the app. The feedback gathered helped fine-tune the app, addressing issues like instruction clarity and user understanding of features. Achieving an SUS score of 82.27 indicated improved usability

Feedback was strong enough that some participants asked when they could actually use it. Error, action, and success colours were praised for clarity, and people specifically liked that the step messaging felt human. Icons around editing and saving still confused people.

We tested with 10 and got a good SUS score, and I'd treat that with more suspicion now. A camera app lives or dies in real conditions; bad light, moving subjects, one hand full. Every test we ran was someone calmly holding a phone in a quiet room.

/case-studies/mphasis-blinkux.title: Voyage Design System | $500M+ in Enterprise Deals
/case-studies/mphasis-blinkux.description: How a token-first design system at Blink UX helped close $500M+ in enterprise deals, cut design turnaround 50%, and scaled to 5 teams and 50+ designers.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
The Design System Behind $100M+ In Enterprise Deals

I joined a pre-sales team at Mphasis whose entire job was winning deals. Anywhere from $1 million to $100 million; by building demos that show a client what their product could look like. Good work, done constantly, by designers all over the org. And every bit of it disappeared the moment it shipped.

A designer would get pulled in for a specific pitch, build ten screens, package them into a prototype, hand it to developers, and the client would see a polished demo. Then that work sat in someone's Outlook or a Teams chat, invisible to the next designer who'd build the same kind of thing from scratch two weeks later for a different client. No shared language, no reusable components, no institutional memory. Just repeated effort, dressed up as bespoke work.
Sole designer responsible for building what became the fix; end to end, from research through a system used company-wide.

Before I opened Figma, I spent two to three months as a researcher, not a designer. I talked to the designers doing this work, the developers building the prototypes, and the salespeople pitching them. Asking what they were actually trying to accomplish, what they built, and for whom.

Every use case, every client type, every solution positioned, and every design pattern used across five to ten years of this team's work. Validated back with the people I'd interviewed, not just written up and filed.
Ideas (everything, good or bad), Product Goals (merged into real-world actions), Users (scenarios)
The finding underneath all of it: these teams' work overlapped constantly. Different clients, same underlying patterns, rebuilt from zero every time.
I spent a week with Mphasis's marketing team learning the actual guidelines; so the system wouldn't just be internally consistent, it would be on-brand the first time, not after a redesign.

Over two to three weeks I studied fifteen existing design systems: Lightning, Manhattan, Material, Apple's Human Interface Guidelines, Uber's, Ant Design, IBM Carbon, and others looking for where their targets overlapped with what Mphasis actually needed, and where nothing out there fit our case at all.

I narrowed that to four systems as primary reference points: Material, IBM Carbon, Lightning, and Uber's; because each had genuinely deep UI kits and component coverage. I built four concept screens themed in Mphasis colors, borrowing structurally from each, and brought them to marketing for a direct reaction: what aligns, what doesn't, what's already how the company shows up elsewhere.
Their answer pointed clearly at one structural direction: Carbon's approach to depth and documentation as the backbone.
I spent three to four months building a system before it touched a single live deal, on a team that measured itself in weekly deal velocity.

That's the tradeoff worth naming. Every week I was building the system instead of shipping deal-specific screens was a week the team's usual output looked slower by the old metric. I made that bet anyway, because the entire premise of the project was that one-off screens were the problem, building more of them faster wasn't a fix, it was more of the disease.

The system, I called it Voyage. Ended up covering roughly 84,000 individual elements, atoms up through molecules, built against 20 marketing-approved brand colors and their accent variations, with full documentation: spacing rules, font hierarchy down to tertiary choices, usage guidance for every component.
Getting it adopted, not just built

Shipping the system wasn't the finish line. I put it back in front of the same designers I'd interviewed at the start and spent one to two months refining it against real feedback: what felt missing, what felt redundant.
Then I kept iterating on a cadence: new versions roughly every two months, driven by what teams actually hit friction on.

About three to four months into adoption, a pattern emerged: sales and business leads increasingly wanted demos visually themed to the specific client being pitched, not a generic Mphasis-branded screen.
So I built variable theme sets into the system: a one-click switch that reskins color, font, and component styling to match any of 20+ major client brands. What had been a rebuild became a toggle.
The clearest example: two months in, teams doing financial-services pitches kept needing better data visualization: tables, charts, pie graphs, etc.
I sat with designers to understand how they were actually building these by hand in Figma, then built proper visualization components so the work became "enter your values"

Clients this touched include Wells Fargo, JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley, Charles Schwab, BlackRock, Corebridge, FedEx, and 20+ other major financial institutions. The system is now being extended with AI-native capability; under NDA at the moment, so that part of the story isn't public yet.

/case-studies/storewell.title: Storewell | HCI Case Study, UT Austin
/case-studies/storewell.description: A grocery inventory app built after shadowing revealed people buy more in person than online, using a fridge-shelf metaphor for stock.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
Grocery management for people with no time

People with busy schedules struggle to buy groceries well and struggle harder to manage what they've bought. Food goes off, money gets wasted, and meal prep gets abandoned somewhere around Wednesday. For students there's a budget dimension, and behind all of it a food-waste problem that's bigger than any one kitchen.
NoWaste (inventory and expiration tracking), FridgePal (fast product entry), Olio (surplus food redistribution). Each solved a slice.
On habits and pain points, deliberately used to narrow scope rather than pile on features.
Ideas (everything, good or bad), Product Goals (merged into real-world actions), Users (scenarios)
For behavioural depth: buying, cooking, storing, and where it breaks down. These fed a WAAD, a flow model, work roles, and later personas.
We tailed people while they actually bought groceries. Not asking — watching.
Shadowing produced the finding the product turned on: people buy more in person than they do online.

That sounds small. It reshapes everything. It means the in-store trip is where over-purchasing originates, which means it's where waste originates, which means an app that only helps you manage what you've already bought is arriving too late. The intervention had to sit before and during the shop, not after it.
International student, first time away from home, no experience buying or storing food, throws a lot away because portion sizes are guesswork.
Student athlete, punishing schedule, cares about a balanced diet, doesn't know what he can cook at home so overspends on restaurants.
The survey told us grocery shopping is an experience for people, not a chore to be abstracted. So we called it a "shopping list," not notes.

Groceries became "stock," because people stock things. And the stocking list UI was built to look like fridge shelves; because that's the mental model people already have, and borrowing it costs nothing.
Five flows: build a shopping list · add bought items to stock · find storing tips · find recipes from what you have · find nearby food banks to share surplus.

People wanted it built. But: the app was too cluttered and complex, icons were hard to find, and language needed to be clearer with onboarding to support it. Storing tips landed well, and people were genuinely excited about video content.

"Too cluttered" is the feedback I'd take most seriously now. We ran good research and then tried to honour all of it at once, five flows in a first release is three too many. The metaphor work was right; the restraint wasn't there yet.

/case-studies/planteria.title: Planteria | UX Prototyping Case Study, UT Austin
/case-studies/planteria.description: A plant care app prototype tested with 8 users across 8 tasks, validated with SUS scoring, from UT Austin's UX Prototyping course.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
A plant care app that learns from its community
People who buy plants mostly don't know how to keep them alive, and the available information is a mess; contradictory, scattered, rarely specific to the plant in front of you.
Our idea had two halves: structure that information properly, then build a community so people posting about how they grow feed the loop and the next person gets better answers.
We studied two products closely. Planta and Nature ID; building a feature list with screenshots to establish a baseline of what people already expect versus where something could stand out.

Ideas (everything, good or bad), Product Goals (merged into real-world actions), Users (scenarios), and Personas — Cassandra, time-poor and curious; Matt, new and interested; Emma, experienced and passionate.
Ideas (everything, good or bad), Product Goals (merged into real-world actions), Users (scenarios)
Feature priority came from where personas overlapped, not from opinion. If all three needed something, it shipped first.
I argued for building our own design system rather than adopting an existing one.

The case against was time, we had none. The case for was that a generic system would have made a plant app feel like every other app, and this product's entire pitch is calm, tactile, close to nature.

Nature-inspired color, earthy tones with green accents. Work Sans for clean modern clarity, Maitree as a serif for character. Then icons, components, and states; filters, forms, textboxes, labels, all with proper active and inactive treatments.

Which is where I spent the most care: changes to existing elements for coherence, bounces for new content entering, sliding page transitions like turning pages in a book. Plus Lottie work; a plant-watering sequence, a checkmark fill that gives an action a small moment of joy.

The onboarding feature helps new users learn the app's key features while authentication ensures privacy and security. Collecting user data allows for personalization and relevant recommendations. The home page and profile feature are tailored to the user's preferences for an enjoyable experience.

The finding plants flow is an efficient way for plant lovers to find, purchase, and care for their plants. It features a vast search with filters, a list of sellers nearby, the ability to add plants to a cart, and the ability to track orders.
A journaling feature in a plant care app can help users track their plant's progress, learn more about their plants, and share their experiences with others.

The results were properly mixed, which is the useful kind. People liked the palette and the micro-animations. They found the home page confusing to navigate and wanted information re-prioritised. Icons and buttons needed simplifying. Plant addition and journaling flows needed cutting down.

I'm still a bit proud of the animation work and a bit suspicious of it. Users liked it; but the same test said the home page was confusing. I'd polished the moments and under-invested in the structure underneath.

/case-studies/makemytrip.title: 72% Faster Checkout for 82M Monthly Users | MakeMyTrip
/case-studies/makemytrip.description: Redesigning checkout for a bus booking platform serving 82M monthly users, improving speed by 72% and cutting drop-off by 34%.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
Cutting checkout time 72% for 82M monthly travellers
I spent my first month not designing anything.

Instead I audited the whole buses and cabs experience, built a flowchart mapping how every part of the company connected, and put together a deck on what I thought was broken. Inconsistent design system, wasted space, visual hierarchy that had quietly given up. I also critiqued GoIbibo's app while I was at it, unprompted.

I presented it expecting to be told which parts I'd got wrong. They put me on the biggest problem in it: users were dropping off hard during seat selection and at payment, and people were coming back after booking with questions because information had never made it onto their screen.
Actually narrowed things down; departure time, bus type, amenities.
Silence reads as broken. Plus ghost loaders, so waiting felt like progress rather than a stall.

This was the hard one. Buses have wildly different layouts: sleeper, semi-sleeper, seater, double-decker; and each needs its own representation. I built a step-by-step mechanism that adapts to whatever layout it's handed, rather than twelve special cases.
Clear coupon actions and a step-by-step payment guide.
The obvious fix was to strip it down. Fewer steps, less information, faster to payment. I didn't, and this is the part worth explaining.

MakeMyTrip needs to cross sell. Flights, hotels, trains, cars; the review page is among the most commercially valuable real estate on the platform. A pure simplification would have improved my metric and quietly cost the business money.

So I restructured when information appeared instead of removing it. Step-by-step navigation, clear transitions, a live review of selections always visible. Cross-sell stayed re-positioned so it never competes with the thing the user came to do.
Same principle, worse conditions: people landing at an airport, stressed, dragging luggage, trying to find their cab.

I built step-by-step illustrated boarding instructions and we A/B tested two versions. Version two won; chosen on support-call volume plus feedback from the staff working the airport booths, not on which one I preferred.
User interviews confirmed people felt less lost hunting for bus information, and support calls dropped.

Looking at that cab onboarding again, would bigger steps have worked better? The distinction between 1, 2, 3 isn't strong enough. And "Take a left from taxi counters to reach the GoIbibo parking and get into your cab" is a mouthful for someone reading it one-handed with a suitcase in the other.

/.title: Samarth Nayyar — Product Designer
/.description: Product Designer, San Francisco. Design systems for AI-native products. 500M+ users. $100M+ in enterprise deals.
h1: Places that let me build things
Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: I build the systems behind products people actually use.
Currently at Blink UX (Mphasis); Previously Paytm, MakeMyTrip, and a hardware startup that somehow convinced the internet to fund us.

I bring consumer-grade craft to software people are forced to use. Enterprise tools, internal dashboards, admin panels; the products people sit inside for eight hours a day and quietly resent. That's where I've spent most of my career, and it's the most interesting design problem I know: nobody chose this software, they just have to live in it.

The other half is design systems; tokens, components, documentation, the infrastructure that decides whether a product stays coherent as it grows. I've built five. One is used by 250+ designers across 12 teams. Another underpins demos that have supported over $100M in enterprise deals.
The design system behind $100M+ in enterprise deals

/case-studies/insider-vibes.title: 0 to 50,000 Paying Users in One Month | Insider Vibes
/case-studies/insider-vibes.description: When COVID killed an events business overnight, I helped build its replacement in six months. 50,000 paying users in month one, 62% came back.
h1: Always up for a conversation about UX, design systems or AI-native tooling
p: Not everyone like's to read to much nowadays (thanks TikTok). See a comic strip?
0 to 50,000 paying users in one month
Tools:  Figma · After Effects · Protopie · Rive · CleverTap

Insider's entire business was offline events. Ticketing, in-person shows, the kind of thing that requires people to be in the same room. Then COVID happened, and the business that had built the company disappeared in about three weeks.

We had six months of runway and no product. Not a slow decline we could plan around, a business model that stopped existing overnight. The mandate was simple to say and hard to do: build something people would pay for, fast, with no idea yet what that something was.

I looked at Clubhouse and Google Meet, not because they were perfect comparisons, but because between them they covered the two things I thought we needed: the intimacy of audio-first rooms and the structure of scheduled, hosted sessions. I broke the comparison into five pieces: audio versus video, exclusivity, community building, moderation, and monetization.

Then user interviews on how people actually attend events, and what changes about that expectation when the event is online. Before any screens, we mapped a value stream. What the product needed to do, and specifically what a user was accomplishing when they came back a second time. I took that to the business and we argued until the design value stream and the business needs actually lined up.
Most platforms design for the third and bolt on tooling for the first two. We designed all three properly, because a community with weak moderation isn't a community for very long.
Three roles, and they needed genuinely different products inside the same product:
Create rooms, manage users, oversee content, set rules.
Support admins, monitor discussions, de-escalate conflict, report upward.
Participate, follow rules, build the community, personalise their profile.
I built the design system plug-and-play from day one, knowing it would slow us down at the start.

The decision that mattered most wasn't a screen. It was building the design system to be genuinely flexible, plug-and-play down to fonts, colors, and components, when every instinct on a six-month runway says just ship the fastest version and fix it later.

That slowed the first few weeks down. It also meant that when engineering rebuilt the entire stack from Angular to React midway through the project, a decision made without me and one I didn't see coming, the interface barely felt it. If I'd built rigid, one-off screens instead of a real system, that migration would have cost us weeks we didn't have.

I also made a smaller call I'd defend again: the poll interaction wasn't the same component reused on every screen. Mobile got a bottom sheet, desktop got a corner box. Small difference, but it meant the feature never felt bolted on to whichever platform wasn't the primary target.

Admins running rooms and setting rules, Moderators keeping sessions on track, Room Joinees showing up to participate. A joining flow that told people upfront what the platform could see and hear from them, camera and mic controls front and center before anyone entered a room, not buried in settings.

An information-dense left panel that resized on interaction, giving people more room to scan detail without a second screen or a separate tab. Animated states for live polls, built in Protopie and Rive, appearing as an unobtrusive bottom sheet on mobile and a corner box on desktop.
Design system underneath all of it
Plug-and-play from day one, translated into React components with the dev team so it could scale past the first version without a redesign.

The bottom half is information-dense and some users want to live in it. Rather than a separate view, the top half shrinks as you scroll so the bottom can breathe. Small thing. Removes a whole navigation step.
A bottom sheet on mobile, an unobtrusive box in the top-right on desktop. Polls should interrupt you just enough to answer and not enough to lose your place in the conversation.

The first number is the one that kept the company alive. The second number is the one I actually care about. Fifty thousand people trying something new during a crisis tells you the offer worked. Sixty-two percent returning tells you the room itself was worth coming back to, not just the novelty of it.

I set up CleverTap to A/B test post-launch, and then moved teams before I ever saw the results. I don't know today which version of which screen actually won. That's a real gap in this story, not a humble-brag, an actual loose thread I'd handle differently now: I'd hand off the test with a clear owner and a date to check back, not just switch it on and walk away.

I'd also push back harder, in hindsight, on being kept out of the Angular-to-React decision. It happened to work out because the system was flexible. It could just as easily not have, and I got lucky that the bet I made for a different reason (plug-and-play components) also happened to save us on a problem I didn't see coming.

/archives/story.title: Samarth Nayyar — Product Designer
/archives/story.description: Product Designer, San Francisco. Design systems for AI-native products. 500M+ users. $100M+ in enterprise deals.
p: Aye good choice on the story version
Who likes being normal innit? Scroll down to go through my journey in a story format.
Born in Lucknow a mischievous child moved to Gurgaon at the age of four where his interest in design was sparked… nah nah that's corny we're not going that far back.

An enthusiastic Samarth Nayyar joined Vellore Institute of Technology in 2016 with his goals set straight, he wanted to be a web developer. The path was planned, to join the most reputed community for developers, Google Developers Student Club VIT. Well, that worked out but a week into the community he was asked to learn design tools to help the short-staffed design team.

A few days after downloading and using the tools followed by taunts of "no design sense", he fell in love with creating experiences before developing them. He asked to be permanently shifted to the design team and focused on building skills for it.

Sitting in his room getting tasks for posters and social media graphics, getting feedback from seniors, and making changes to learn would be the summary for the first 6 months. Then came the flagship event where he met all the other members and made lifelong friends.

Since that day he never skipped a meeting and started getting involved in projects with other developers and seniors to venture into the field of UI/UX and motion graphics. The next year was filled with tagging along seniors in projects to learn the processes.

Soon due to the commitment of senior members and as a reward for his commitment to the design team, he informally took charge of the design team handling the learning of new members and managing the branding of the whole community.
This was followed by a few UI/UX and branding projects which were led by him. Some of these projects were:
A branding project to announce the board of GDSC VIT of 2017.
A UI/UX project for an application designed to share images.
During his second and third years in university after learning the basics of design from the community, he wanted to gain some industrial experience.

He joined a startup as a part-time Motion Graphics and Product Designer, where he worked for 18 months to hone his skills in the field of design. While also learned about the marketing and business side of things to combine with various people from diverse backgrounds to launch a product called KAI, which raised $100,000+ in crowdfunding on Indiegogo.
The first year was completed and the plan was to go industrial experience as an intern at a reputed company to see how things work in the real world with time crunch and deadlines.

He joined ofbusiness in Gurgaon for a period of 2 months as a Motion Graphics and Product Designer. Helping create branding for a sub-brand and creating videos to attract investors for the next round of funding.
SECOND INTERNSHIP AT AIRTEL PAYMENTS BANK

After completing two years at the university, he had more knowledge about the field of design and wanted to get experience at a company which has a clever design team with a focus on building applications.
He joined Airtel Payments Bank for 2 months as a product designer helping them rebuild their merchant application.
After 2 years of being part of the Google Developers Student Club community, he was named as the new community lead. Responsible for guiding the community in a new direction.
Over the next 12 months, he focused on improving the community's output in events and projects. Conducting over ten events in a year.

Also working on 20+ projects in a calendar year with a few of them getting large-scale recognition due to being partnered with the University, The Local Police, The Government and NGOs. A couple of them are highlighted below:
Cultivating Hope: Empowering Adolescents Through 'Hope House'
This case study explores the collaborative project titled "Hope House," undertaken in partnership with a NGO based in Vellore.
This case study delves into the collaborative project known as "Election Eye," a groundbreaking initiative conducted in partnership with the Tamil Nadu Police.

A few months after becoming the lead due to the community and his contributions to the Google Student circle, he was selected as one of the top 5 performing leads out of 500+ leads over the world for the year.

He was invited to attend Google I/O 2019 and visit the Google office in California. He spent 15 days in the United States sponsored by Google to learn more about communities and Google with 4 other leads.

After 3 years of arduous work in the community, he was selected by the university for their latest project called "VIT Hack" a large-scale international hackathon and the university wanted the performing students in the university to host it.

He was selected as the Design Lead and was involved in creating a branding for the whole project from scratch while also building a design system which would be used for years to come by the university.

Coming together with 8 other people who were the best in their field, they conducted a Hackathon unlike any other in the university. People from 10+ countries, 20+ speakers, multiple events, and 2 days of continuous product building.
While in the second last semester of undergraduate, the search for an internship during the semester started and a list of about ten companies was made to target.

The aim was to get experience in a company whose design team and culture inspired him. One of those companies was MakeMyTrip and after a few interviews, he was given an opportunity to work as a Product Design Intern in the Bus and Cabs department.
He worked on improving the visual identity of the cabs product and re-imagining the user flows for booking buses to make it easier for the users reducing customer failure rates.
Making the most out of Breaks

During his break after his internship at MakeMyTrip, he has a short stint as a freelance Product Designer at Winuall. He was responsible for creating a contemporary design system and branding for the product, then incorporating it into their admin and student products.
Successfully a Full Time Product Designer
2 YEARS AT PAYTM AND PAYTM INSIDER

After his internships, he moved into a full-time role as a Product Designer at Paytm Insider. His role here was to build design systems for the new products launched during covid to help the company make the best out of the digital space. Read more about the projects below:

The ultimate social platform where you can build and join vibrant communities of like-minded individuals. Engage in meaningful discussions, earn experience levels, and even participate in exciting community events through polls.
Time to get Education in Design
4 internships, 1 full-time position, multiple freelance projects, and 2+ years of experience in designing. He decided it was time to get educated and clear the concepts about the cores of designing.
He applied to a few top universities for a Master's in the field of UX Design and got selected by the University of Texas at Austin.

During his first semester and second semester he has been getting part-time experience as a Graphic Designer for a department at the university. Learning about the culture and work style of a different country while also adding Graphic Design experience to his arsenal.

During my summer internship at ThinkQ AI in Dallas, Texas, I had the opportunity to make a significant impact on the user experience (UX) of our product. Over the course of four months, I worked remotely to implement UX flows that transformed early-stage ideas into tangible solutions.

One of my key achievements was overhauling the design system, setting the stage for alpha testing with potential customers. Throughout the internship, I honed my skills in wireframing, user interface design, and tools like Figma and After Effects, while also contributing to graphic design, UX, and web design projects. It was an exciting and rewarding experience that allowed me to apply my UX design skills in a real-world context.
Capstone Project at Carolinas Psychiatric Institute

Soon to graduate and during my final semester as University of Texas at Austin I joined Carolinas Psychiatric Institute as a Product Designer to help merge the gap between Artificial Intelligence and Medical Practitioners.Responsible for creating a design system that embodies trust with professional looks to help onboarding doctors onto the platform to build a community where medical professionals can help each other help the world around them.
